chapters.title: Unit 4: Functions Involving Parameters, Vectors, and Matrices

terms.def: Half the distance between the greatest and least values of a sinusoidal function, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>min</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\max - \min}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>: how far the graph reaches above and below its midline. It is never negative.

The length of a piece of a circle. A central angle of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> degrees cuts off the fraction <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>θ</mi><mn>360</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\theta}{360}</annotation></semantics></math> of the circumference, so the arc has length <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>θ</mi><mn>360</mn></mfrac><mo>⋅</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s = \frac{\theta}{360} \cdot 2\pi r</annotation></semantics></math>.
A sequence with a common difference d: each term is the previous term plus d, so a_n = a_0 + dn, or a_n = a_k + d(n - k) from any known term a_k. Its terms change by equal amounts.
terms.topicTitle: Change in Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences

terms.def: The average rate of change of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> on <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}</annotation></semantics></math>, the slope of the line through <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a, f(a))</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(b, f(b))</annotation></semantics></math>, in output units per input unit.

The rule for expanding a power of a sum, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a + b)^n</annotation></semantics></math>: the terms run from <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^n</annotation></semantics></math> down to <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^n</annotation></semantics></math>, and their coefficients are row <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> of Pascal's triangle, where each entry is the sum of the two entries above it.
terms.topicTitle: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions

terms.def: The complex conjugate of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a + bi</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a - bi</annotation></semantics></math>. Their product, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^2 + b^2</annotation></semantics></math>, is real.

A number <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a + bi</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> are real and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is the imaginary unit, with <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i^2 = -1</annotation></semantics></math>. <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> is the real part and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> the imaginary part.

A zero of a polynomial that may be real or non-real. A polynomial of degree <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> has <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> complex zeros counting multiplicity; with real coefficients, non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>±</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a \pm bi</annotation></semantics></math>.

A function built by using the output of one function as the input of another. The composite <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(g(x))</annotation></semantics></math>, also written <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>∘</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(f \circ g)(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, applies <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> first and then <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>.
A graph is concave up on an interval when its rate of change is increasing there (it bends upward), and concave down when its rate of change is decreasing (it bends downward).

A curve made by slicing a double cone with a plane: a parabola, an ellipse (a circle is a special one) or a hyperbola. Ellipse: (x − h)²/a² + (y − k)²/b² = 1. Hyperbola: (x − h)²/a² − (y − k)²/b² = 1, with asymptotes y − k = ±(b/a)(x − h).
Two quantities covary when a change in one goes with a change in the other, as the input and output of a function do.

The highest power of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in a polynomial with a nonzero coefficient. A nonzero constant has degree <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change

terms.def: For a 2 × 2 matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d), the number ad − bc. Its absolute value is the area of the parallelogram made by the columns. The inverse matrix A⁻¹, with AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I, exists exactly when the determinant is not 0, and then it is (1/(ad − bc)) times the matrix with rows (d, −b) and (−c, a).
terms.topicTitle: The Inverse and Determinant of a Matrix

terms.def: The set of inputs a function accepts. For a formula, every real number that gives a real output: no zero denominators and no square roots of negative numbers.

What the outputs of a function do as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \to \infty</annotation></semantics></math> and as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \to -\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. For a polynomial it matches its leading term: even degree, both ends the same way; odd degree, opposite ways.

The equation <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2</annotation></semantics></math> of the circle with center <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(h, k)</annotation></semantics></math> and radius <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>: it says the point <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x, y)</annotation></semantics></math> is at distance <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> from the center. The circle of radius 1 centered at the origin is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^2 + y^2 = 1</annotation></semantics></math>.

Different ways of writing the same exponential function, found with the exponent rules: 2^(x + 3) = 8(2)^x, 5(4)^x = 5(2)^(2x), (1/3)^x = 3^(-x). A horizontal translation equals a vertical dilation, and a horizontal dilation equals a change of base.
aka: change of base of an exponential

terms.def: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is an even function if <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(-x) = f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> (graph symmetric about the <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-axis) and an odd function if <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(-x) = -f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> (graph symmetric about the origin).

The laws of exponents for a positive base <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>⋅</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^m \cdot b^n = b^{m + n}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{b^m}{b^n} = b^{m - n}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(b^m)^n = b^{mn}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^0 = 1</annotation></semantics></math>, a negative exponent <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^{-n} = \frac{1}{b^n}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a rational exponent <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mroot><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></mroot><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^{m/n} = (\sqrt[n]{b})^m</annotation></semantics></math>.

An exponential equation has the unknown in an exponent, such as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>⋅</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>48</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3 \cdot 2^x = 48</annotation></semantics></math>; a logarithmic equation has it inside a logarithm, such as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_2(x + 1) = 3</annotation></semantics></math>. Each is solved by undoing one function with its inverse.
terms.topicTitle: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations and Inequalities

terms.def: A function f(x) = ab^x with a not 0, b > 0 and b not 1: the input is in the exponent. Over equal-length input intervals its outputs change by a constant ratio. If b > 1 it shows exponential growth; if 0 < b < 1, exponential decay.
terms.topicTitle: Change in Linear and Exponential Functions

terms.def: A function model of the form f(t) = ab^t, where a is the initial value and b the growth (or decay) factor per unit of t. It is built from an initial value and a ratio, from two data points, or by exponential regression on a calculator.
terms.topicTitle: Exponential Function Context and Data Modeling

terms.def: A value produced while solving that does not satisfy the original equation, often because it makes the input of a logarithm zero or negative, or makes <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^x</annotation></semantics></math> negative. Every candidate must be checked in the original.
terms.topicTitle: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations and Inequalities

terms.def: A polynomial written as a product of factors, such as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2x(x - 3)(x + 1)</annotation></semantics></math>. Each linear factor shows a zero. Standard form, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2x^3 - 4x^2 - 6x</annotation></semantics></math>, lists the terms by degree and shows the leading term and so the end behavior.
terms.topicTitle: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions

terms.def: Writing an expression as a product: take out a common factor, use patterns such as the difference of squares <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)</annotation></semantics></math> and the sum or difference of cubes, or factor by grouping.

The number of cycles a periodic function completes per unit of input: the reciprocal of the period. A period of 4 seconds is a frequency of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{4}</annotation></semantics></math> cycle per second.

A rule that gives each input exactly one output. <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(3) = 7</annotation></semantics></math> means the input <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> gives the output <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7</annotation></semantics></math>.

A function chosen to describe how one quantity in a real situation depends on another, such as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(t)</annotation></semantics></math> for height after <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> seconds. It is chosen from the pattern in the data and from the context, and used to predict and explain.
terms.topicTitle: Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation

terms.def: A change to a function that moves, stretches or flips its graph, made by adding to or multiplying the input or the output. The new function is written in terms of the old one, such as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x) = 2f(x - 3) + 1</annotation></semantics></math>.

A sequence with a common ratio r: each term is the previous term times r, so g_n = g_0 r^n, or g_n = g_k r^(n - k) from any known term g_k. Its terms change by amounts that are themselves multiplied by r.
terms.topicTitle: Change in Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences

terms.def: The global maximum is the greatest output over the whole domain; the global minimum is the least. On a closed interval, compare the local extremum values and the endpoint values.
terms.topicTitle: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change

terms.def: All the points <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x, f(x))</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in the domain, drawn in the plane: inputs across, outputs up.

The base b of an exponential function in context: the factor the output is multiplied by for each unit of input. A percent change r (as a decimal) gives the growth factor b = 1 + r: a 4% increase is b = 1.04, and a 15% decrease is the decay factor b = 0.85.

A single point missing from a graph. A rational function has a hole at <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = a</annotation></semantics></math> when <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x - a)</annotation></semantics></math> divides the numerator at least as many times as the denominator; its height is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></munder><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to a} r(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, found by cancelling the factor and evaluating.

A line <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = c</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to \infty} r(x) = c</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to -\infty} r(x) = c</annotation></semantics></math>. For a rational function: the ratio of leading coefficients when the degrees are equal, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 0</annotation></semantics></math> when the denominator's degree is greater.

The side of a right triangle across from the right angle, and its longest side. The other two sides, the legs, are named from an acute angle <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>: the opposite side is across from <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, the adjacent side touches <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.

The function <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(x) = x</annotation></semantics></math>, which returns every input unchanged. Composing any function with it, in either order, gives the same function back.

A relationship between x and y given by an equation, such as x² + xy + y² = 7, rather than by a formula y = f(x). Its graph is every point that satisfies the equation; it may or may not be the graph of a function of x.

<math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is increasing on an interval if larger inputs give larger outputs there: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo><</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a) < f(b)</annotation></semantics></math> whenever <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a < b</annotation></semantics></math> in the interval. It is decreasing if <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>></mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a) > f(b)</annotation></semantics></math> whenever <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a < b</annotation></semantics></math>.

A way to write a stretch of the number line by its ends: a bracket for an included end, a parenthesis for an excluded end or for <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">±</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1, 4)</annotation></semantics></math> means <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1 \le x < 4</annotation></semantics></math>. A closed interval includes both ends; an open interval includes neither.

The function <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> that undoes <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}(b) = a</annotation></semantics></math> exactly when <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a) = b</annotation></semantics></math>. It exists when <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is one-to-one (each output comes from exactly one input); then <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(f^{-1}(x)) = x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}(f(x)) = x</annotation></semantics></math>.

An exponential function <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = b^x</annotation></semantics></math> and the logarithm with the same base, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = \log_b x</annotation></semantics></math>, undo each other: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_b(b^x) = x</annotation></semantics></math> for every <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^{\log_b x} = x</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x > 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Their graphs are reflections across <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = x</annotation></semantics></math>.

Inverse proportion: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = \frac{k}{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, so the product <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">xy</annotation></semantics></math> stays constant and doubling <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> halves <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>. An inverse-square law, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>k</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = \frac{k}{x^2}</annotation></semantics></math>, divides <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> by <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> when <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> doubles, as for light intensity and distance.

The inverse sine, inverse cosine and inverse tangent functions, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin^{-1} x</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos^{-1} x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>tan</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan^{-1} x</annotation></semantics></math> (also written <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arcsin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arcsin x</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arccos x</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arctan x</annotation></semantics></math>). Each takes a ratio and returns an angle: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>tan</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">[</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math> (open for tangent), <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0, \pi]</annotation></semantics></math>. They are inverses, not reciprocals.

The term with the highest power of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_n x^n</annotation></semantics></math>; its coefficient <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_n</annotation></semantics></math> is the leading coefficient.
terms.topicTitle: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change

terms.def: Limit notation describes where outputs go: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = \infty</annotation></semantics></math> means that as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> increases without bound, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> increases without bound. Write the function, its input, where the input goes and where the outputs go.

A statement that one quantity is less than (or greater than) another, such as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3 - 2x > 7</annotation></semantics></math>. A linear inequality, with the variable to the first power, is solved like an equation, but the sign flips when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number.

A rule that sends each vector ⟨x, y⟩ to ⟨ax + by, cx + dy⟩: multiplication by the matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d). Its columns are the images of ⟨1, 0⟩ and ⟨0, 1⟩. It keeps the origin fixed and lines straight, and multiplies every area by the absolute value of its determinant.

A local maximum is an output at least as large as the outputs at all nearby inputs; a local minimum is one at most as large. They occur where a function switches between increasing and decreasing, or at an included endpoint.
terms.topicTitle: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change

terms.def: The exponent a base needs to produce a number: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_b c = a</annotation></semantics></math> means <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>a</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^a = c</annotation></semantics></math> (for <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b > 0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b \ne 1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c > 0</annotation></semantics></math>). The common logarithm <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log c</annotation></semantics></math> has base <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math>; the natural logarithm <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln c</annotation></semantics></math> has base <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>.

A function of the form <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) = a\log_b x</annotation></semantics></math> (with <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b > 0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b \ne 1</annotation></semantics></math>), or a transformation of it. It is defined for <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x > 0</annotation></semantics></math>, has the vertical asymptote <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, is always increasing or always decreasing, has one concavity and no extrema.

A function model of the form <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = a + b\ln x</annotation></semantics></math> (or with another base), used when equal factors in the input go with equal changes in the output. It is built from two points or by logarithmic regression.
terms.topicTitle: Logarithmic Function Context and Data Modeling

terms.def: A scale on which numbers are placed by their logarithms, so equal distances stand for equal factors (often factors of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math>). It shows values of very different sizes on one axis.

A rectangular array of numbers with m rows and n columns (dimensions m × n). Matrices of the same dimensions add entry by entry. The product AB is defined when A has as many columns as B has rows; the entry in row i, column j is row i of A times column j of B, multiplied entry by entry and added.

A matrix used as a function on vectors: input v, output Av. Doing B and then A is the composition of linear transformations, with matrix AB (the first move on the right). The inverse function has matrix A⁻¹, which exists exactly when det A is not 0.

The horizontal line halfway between the greatest and least values of a sinusoidal function, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>min</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = \frac{\max + \min}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. The graph oscillates around it.

A condition a function model takes for granted, such as a sheet having no thickness or a rate staying constant. Assumptions include the restricted domain (or contextual domain) and range: only the inputs and outputs the situation allows.
terms.topicTitle: Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation

terms.def: If <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x - a)^k</annotation></semantics></math> is a factor of a polynomial and no higher power is, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> is a zero of multiplicity <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>. The graph crosses the <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-axis at a zero of odd multiplicity and touches it at a zero of even multiplicity (a double zero has multiplicity <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>).
The number e, about 2.71828, used as the base of an exponential function, as in f(x) = e^x. It arises naturally when growth happens continuously; a calculator has a key for it.

The behavior of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> approaches <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> from one side: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> from the left, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> from the right. At a vertical asymptote each is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\infty</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>.

The U-shaped graph of a quadratic function; it opens up when <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a > 0</annotation></semantics></math> and down when <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a < 0</annotation></semantics></math>, and is symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex.
terms.topicTitle: Quadratics: Zeros and the Quadratic Formula

terms.def: An extra input variable, often written t, that both coordinates of a curve depend on. Each value of the parameter picks out one point, and increasing it sets the order in which the points are traced.

A circle or line written with parametric equations. The circle with center (h, k) and radius r: x(t) = h + r cos t, y(t) = k + r sin t, which goes once around counterclockwise from (h + r, k) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π. The segment from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2): x(t) = x1 + (x2 − x1)t, y(t) = y1 + (y2 − y1)t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.
A function f(t) = (x(t), y(t)) that sends each value of a parameter t to the point (x(t), y(t)). As t runs through an interval, the points trace a curve with a direction of travel.

For a parametric function (x(t), y(t)) on an interval [t1, t2]: the average rate of change of x, the average rate of change of y, and their quotient, the change in y over the change in x, which is the slope of the segment joining the two points.
terms.topicTitle: Parametric Functions and Rates of Change
aka: rate of change of a parametric function

terms.def: A parametric function (x(t), y(t)) that traces a given curve. For example, (t, f(t)) parametrizes y = f(x), and (h + a cos t, k + b sin t) parametrizes an ellipse. A curve has many parametrizations, differing in start, direction and speed.

A function whose outputs repeat at regular intervals of input: there is a positive number <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x + P) = f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> for every <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. The smallest such <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> is the period, the length of one full cycle.

The horizontal translation of a sinusoidal function. In <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= a\sin(b(\theta + c)) + d</annotation></semantics></math> the graph of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\sin(b\theta) + d</annotation></semantics></math> moves left <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> units when <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c > 0</annotation></semantics></math> and right <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|c|</annotation></semantics></math> units when <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c < 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Factor <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> out of the input before reading it.
A function that uses different formulas on different parts of its domain. To evaluate it, find the piece whose condition the input meets.
Motion of an object in a flat plane, described by a parametric function: at time t the object is at (x(t), y(t)). It moves right where x(t) increases and up where y(t) increases.
A point where a graph changes concavity: its rate of change switches from increasing to decreasing, or from decreasing to increasing.
terms.topicTitle: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change

terms.def: Point-slope form <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)</annotation></semantics></math> is the line through <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_1, y_1)</annotation></semantics></math> with slope <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>; slope-intercept form <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = mx + b</annotation></semantics></math> has slope <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-intercept <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, b)</annotation></semantics></math>.

A way to name a point by its distance <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> from the pole (the origin) and the angle <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> from the polar axis (the positive <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-axis): <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(r, \theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. They convert with <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = r\cos\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = r\sin\theta</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^2 = x^2 + y^2</annotation></semantics></math>. A negative <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> points the opposite way, and each point has many polar names.

terms.term: polar form of a complex number
terms.def: The form <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> of a complex number <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a + bi</annotation></semantics></math>, from the polar coordinates of the point <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a, b)</annotation></semantics></math> in the complex plane: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}</annotation></semantics></math> is its distance from <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> its angle.

A function <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = f(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> whose input is an angle and whose output is a signed distance from the pole. Its graph in the polar plane is all points <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(f(\theta), \theta)</annotation></semantics></math>; families include circles, limaçons and cardioids (<math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = a + b\cos\theta</annotation></semantics></math>) and rose curves (<math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = a\sin(n\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = a\cos(n\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>).

A sum of terms <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ax^n</annotation></semantics></math> with whole-number powers <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>, such as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^3 + x^2 - 7x + 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

A function <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>⋯</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= a_n x^n + \cdots + a_1 x + a_0</annotation></semantics></math> with whole-number powers and real coefficients.
terms.topicTitle: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change

terms.def: A way to divide one polynomial by another, like long division of numbers: divide the leading terms, multiply, subtract, repeat. It writes the dividend as divisor times quotient plus remainder, where the remainder has lower degree than the divisor.
terms.topicTitle: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions

terms.def: Rules for rewriting logarithms, for positive <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>: product <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_b(xy)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \log_b x + \log_b y</annotation></semantics></math>; quotient <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_b \frac{x}{y}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \log_b x - \log_b y</annotation></semantics></math>; power <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_b(x^n) = n\log_b x</annotation></semantics></math>; change of base <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_b x</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\log_a x}{\log_a b}</annotation></semantics></math>.

The identity <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1</annotation></semantics></math>, true because <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\cos x, \sin x)</annotation></semantics></math> is on the unit circle, and its forms <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>tan</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>sec</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>cot</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>csc</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 + \cot^2 x = \csc^2 x</annotation></semantics></math>.

The solutions of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ax^2 + bx + c = 0</annotation></semantics></math> are <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>±</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}</annotation></semantics></math>. The discriminant <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^2 - 4ac</annotation></semantics></math> tells how many are real: two, one or none. Completing the square rewrites a quadratic in vertex form.
terms.topicTitle: Quadratics: Zeros and the Quadratic Formula

terms.def: A function <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Its graph is a parabola.
terms.topicTitle: Quadratics: Zeros and the Quadratic Formula

terms.def: A unit of angle measure: an angle's radian measure is the length of the arc it cuts off divided by the radius. A full turn is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> radians, so <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> radians <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mo>∘</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 180^\circ</annotation></semantics></math>. On the unit circle, an angle of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> radians cuts off an arc of length <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.

A root written with the radical sign, such as the square root <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>b</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{b}</annotation></semantics></math> or the cube root <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mroot><mi>b</mi><mn>3</mn></mroot></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt[3]{b}</annotation></semantics></math>. The <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>th root of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> is the number whose <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>th power is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>, and it equals the rational exponent <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^{1/n}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The set of outputs a function produces as the input runs through its domain.
How fast a function's output changes compared with its input. A positive rate means the output rises as the input rises; a negative rate means it falls.

How <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> changes as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> changes for a polar function. The average rate of change of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> on <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{r(b) - r(a)}{b - a}</annotation></semantics></math>, in units per radian. The distance from the origin, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|r|</annotation></semantics></math>, increases where <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is positive and increasing or negative and decreasing, and decreases otherwise.
terms.topicTitle: Rates of Change in Polar Functions
aka: average rate of change of r

terms.def: A quotient of two polynomials, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}</annotation></semantics></math>, undefined where <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(x) = 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Simplify by cancelling common factors; the inputs excluded from the original stay excluded.

A function <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(x) = \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> are polynomials and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> is not the zero polynomial.

An inequality such as <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \ge 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Solve it with a sign chart: split the number line at the zeros of the numerator and the denominator, test one input in each interval, include zeros only for <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>≤</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\le</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>≥</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ge</annotation></semantics></math>, and never include an excluded input.

A flip of a graph. <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x) = -f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is the reflection across the <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-axis (outputs change sign); <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x) = f(-x)</annotation></semantics></math> is the reflection across the <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-axis (inputs change sign).

Fitting a model of a chosen type (linear, quadratic, cubic, quartic, and later exponential and others) to all the data at once with a calculator, which picks the constants that make the model closest to the data. Linear regression and quadratic regression are the common cases.

Actual value minus predicted value at a data point: positive where a model underestimates, negative where it overestimates. A residual plot graphs the residuals against the input; an appropriate model leaves small residuals with no pattern.

The secant, cosecant and cotangent functions: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sec</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>csc</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cot</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cot x = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}</annotation></semantics></math>. Each has vertical asymptotes where its denominator is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>. Secant and cosecant have range <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo>,</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>∪</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)</annotation></semantics></math> and period <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math>; cotangent has range <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(-\infty, \infty)</annotation></semantics></math> and period <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: The Secant, Cosecant, and Cotangent Functions

terms.def: A line through two points <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a, f(a))</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(b, f(b))</annotation></semantics></math> of a graph. Its slope, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}</annotation></semantics></math>, is the average rate of change of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> on <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions

terms.def: For outputs at equal input steps, the changes in the first differences (the changes in output). Constant second differences mean the values fit a quadratic function.
terms.topicTitle: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions

terms.def: A graph with one axis, usually the vertical one, on a logarithmic scale. Exponential data <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>⋅</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = a \cdot b^x</annotation></semantics></math> appear as a straight line on it, with slope <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log b</annotation></semantics></math> and intercept <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log a</annotation></semantics></math>.
An ordered list of numbers, called terms, written a_0, a_1, a_2, ... or starting at a_1. It is a function whose inputs are whole numbers (the positions), so its graph is a set of separate dots.
terms.topicTitle: Change in Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences

terms.def: The graph of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = \sin\theta</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = \cos\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, traced from the unit circle: sine is the point's height and cosine its horizontal position. Both repeat every <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and oscillate between <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>; the cosine curve is the sine curve shifted <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to the left.

The sine and cosine functions, and with them tangent, defined for any angle <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> in standard position: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos\theta</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin\theta</annotation></semantics></math> are the <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>- and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-coordinates of the point where the terminal ray meets the unit circle, and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is the slope of the terminal ray.

A function whose graph is the graph of sine (or cosine) after vertical and horizontal dilations and translations: a smooth wave that oscillates evenly about a horizontal line. Described by its amplitude, midline, period and frequency.

A sinusoidal function <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\sin(b(t + c)) + d</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\cos(b(t + c)) + d</annotation></semantics></math> used to describe a periodic context. Its constants come from the greatest and least values, the period and one landmark time, or from a sinusoidal regression on data. It is valid on the domain the context supports.
terms.topicTitle: Sinusoidal Function Context and Data Modeling
